claims.claim: Brand equity is the added value a brand has over a substitute; if a consumer will pay more for one similar product over another because of the brand, that difference represents its brand equity.

The American Marketing Association describes brand equity as the intangible value a brand holds in the minds of consumers, reflecting how well the brand is recognized, perceived, and trusted; strong brand equity equates to higher customer loyalty and increased market share.
Positive brand equity leads customers to willingly pay a price premium for a brand's products even when they could get a similar product from a competitor for less.
Brand equity builds when products are memorable, easily recognizable, and superior or reliable in quality, reinforced by consistent marketing and positive customer experiences.
Brand loyalty ranges from switchers to hard-core loyals; loyal customers repeatedly purchase the brand and advocate for it to others, extending word-of-mouth marketing.

There is no single measure of brand value; the valuation process is subjective and may be based on brand visibility, customer loyalty, and perception of the brand, along with financial measures such as revenue.
Brand equity commands higher prices, so national brands typically charge higher prices than their private-label counterparts.
Licensed brands and co-brands gain brand recognition and benefit from the equity of the brands involved in the arrangement.

conflictingEvidence.note: Sources agree on the core concept (added value beyond the product) but frame it differently: OpenStax defines equity relative to a substitute product, the AMA frames it as intangible value in consumers' minds, and Investopedia frames it as a value premium over a generic equivalent. These are complementary framings of one concept, not contradictions; the lesson presents the shared working definition with attribution to OpenStax and the AMA.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, 9.5 Branding and Brand Development
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20230204191557 (openstax.org blocks direct fetch). Defines brand equity as the additional value a brand has over a substitute and the price premium as its measure; presents Keller's customer-based brand equity model (identity, meaning, feelings/judgments, resonance); notes brand value has no single measure and that valuation is subjective (visibility, loyalty, perception, revenue); states brand equity commands higher prices for national brands; covers trademarks and licensed/co-brand equity. Supports the working definition, the price-premium measure, the equity-vs-value distinction, and the partnerships benefit.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, 9.6 Forms of Brand Development, Brand Loyalty, and Brand Metrics
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture 20230204183951. Describes four loyalty categories (switchers, shifting loyals, split loyals, hard-core loyals), that loyal customers purchase and advocate for the brand, and brand metrics (brand lift, brand engagement, brand preference). Supports the loyalty sign of equity and the resilience benefit.

sourceRecords.title: Branding (topic page: What is a Brand? / What is Brand Equity?)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Defines a brand as any distinctive feature like a name, term, design, or symbol that identifies goods or services, and brand equity as the intangible value a brand holds in the minds of consumers, reflecting recognition, perception, and trust, with strong equity equating to higher loyalty and market share. Supports the working definition and the trust framing.

sourceRecords.title: Brand Equity
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Defines brand equity as the value premium a company generates from a product with a recognizable name compared to a generic equivalent; identifies three components (consumer perception, positive or negative effects, resulting value); states equity builds from memorable, recognizable, reliable products and consistent marketing, and that customers willingly pay a price premium. Supports the price-premium sign, the build path, and the risks framing.
